newsitem.title: USA: Stock prices hinge on earnings outlook - Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: Stock prices hinge on earnings outlook - Greenspan.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Aaln Greenspan, who just last week suggested that stock prices may be too high, said on Wednesday that he did not know what the outlook for the market was.

In comments to the National Association of Busness Economists, the central bank chief even went so far as to say that the market might be reasonably priced, provided that analysts' forecasts of future corporate earnings prove right.
"I don't know what the stock price outlook is," he said.

But, he added, "It's pretty obvious that if you look at a normal pricing model for stocks, what you get is a not unreasonable level of prices if the earnings forecasts which the analysts are publishing are accurate."
"Because if they are accurate ... at these interest (rate) levels, the market is properly priced, as best we can judge,' he said.
Arguing that what was important for the stock market was whether corporate profit margins will continue to rise, Greenspan said that such margins are "quite high" when compared with 1991.
On the other hand, he added, they are significantly below what they were in the 1960's, when inflation was about where it is now. Underlying inflation is now below three percent.

Greenspan said the Fed was committed to doing all it can to ensure maximum sustainable economic growth, adding that low inflation or "preferably stable prices" were a necessary condition for achieving that.
"In order to evaluate where the pressures are on the price level, you've got to look at the whole structure of the system," Greenspan said.

Among the data he looks at, Greenspan said, are money supply -- "even with its deficiencies" --, gold prices -- "the only truly monetary metal out there which captures changes in price expectations as well as anything we've got" -- and the Treasury's new index-linked debt.
"What I'm saying is that we have got to increase, as the complexity of the economy increases, all the various tools we employ for evaluating monetary policy," he said.
As he did on Tuesday, Greenspan denied trying to talk down the stock market by suggesting first in December and then last week that prices might be too high.
"You cannot affect the broad level of equity values by jawboning," he said.
The Fed chief said that he knew that his mere mention of the stock market in a speech in December would affect equity prices. But he did not know by how much.
Greenspan has come in for some sharp criticism for his comments from investors and analysts who have accused him of meddling in a market in which he has no business doing so.

The central bank Chairman though defended his comments, saying that the Fed needed to take account of what he called "balance sheet forces" because of their increasing importance in trying to gauge the future direction of the economy.
Greenspan said that markets, especially the stock market, very rarely "peak out" in response to any particular event.
"What tends to happen is that everyone gets increasingly bullish and that everyone is committed and there's no one left to buy when somebody wants to sell," he said.
